clue.text: It's enforced as naughty child does wrong

indicators.note: something done wrong is done out of order, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: A rule is laid down because a naughty child keeps misbehaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A penalty that is imposed has been enforced on someone by authority.

clue.text: My admission of being dated produces standoff

parts.note: passé means out of date, completing the confession

explanation.surface: Someone confessing they are old-fashioned brings negotiations to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase 'My admission of being dated' is the confession I'M PASSÉ, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a deadlock where neither side can advance, the same thing as a standoff.

clue.text: Tender pair, shortly before proposal

parts.note: pr is the standard abbreviation for pair

explanation.surface: A loving couple, just before a marriage proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective for the pair; it is the verb meaning to offer.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender something is to hold it out for acceptance, which is what proffer means.

clue.text: Proceed arrogantly, supporting member

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to walk with a swagger
second meaning: a brace or bar in a framework

explanation.surface: A pompous party member parades about backing the leadership.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to swagger; as a noun it is a structural bar bearing a load.

clue.text: Friar from Caribbean island

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a member of the order founded by St Dominic

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, fair because the answer is also an adjective meaning belonging to Dominica
definitions.meaning: second meaning: belonging to Dominica or the ... Republic

explanation.surface: A monk who hails from somewhere in the West Indies.
explanation.definitionFit: The Black Friars are the religious order of St Dominic, and the same word describes natives of Dominica.

clue.text: Lack of faith he's shown in source of notes

indicators.note: being shown in something places one thing inside another

explanation.surface: Someone's unbelief is revealed by the composer of a musical score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' suggests music, but here they are banknotes, and an ATM is a cash machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Atheism is disbelief in any god, an absence of religious faith.

clue.text: Passes tests, with odd exceptions, producing advantage

indicators.note: excepting the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones in place

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Getting through exams, bar a few odd failures, gives you an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful quality or resource, something that gives an advantage.

clue.text: Awfully rough girl's timer with tiny moving parts

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the following letters are disordered

parts.note: a lass is a girl; the 's means 'is', joining on

explanation.surface: A rough girl is timing something with a gadget full of small moving pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An hourglass times by trickling grains of sand, the tiny moving parts, from one bulb to the other.

clue.text: Popular Conservative policy that's not on the level

parts.note: a party line is its policy

explanation.surface: A Tory policy that voters like turns out to be dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on the level' suggests shady politics; literally, it describes a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: An incline is a slope, ground that is literally not level.

clue.text: I'm turning up original tunes for record

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means reading upwards, so the word is flipped
an original version is a newly invented one, so the letters are freshly arranged

explanation.surface: A musician arrives with new songs to put on a disc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a disc or a verb; it is the noun for the written account of a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutes are the official written record of what was said at a meeting.

clue.text: Weight attached to expert coder's work

parts.note: a gram is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A weight is fixed to something a specialist software writer made.
explanation.walkthrough: The weight is attached after the expert, so its letters come second.
explanation.definitionFit: A program is the software a coder writes; this spelling is the computing one.

clue.text: After initial course, study little

parts.note: soup is often the first course of a meal
to con is to study carefully

explanation.surface: Once your first lesson is done, you don't study much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests education, but it is part of a meal; to con is an old word for to learn by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A soupçon is a very small amount, a little, as in a soupçon of garlic.

clue.text: Second twist of fate, even after installing new precautionary measure

indicators.note: to install something is to put it inside, so one piece goes within another
a twist distorts shape, so the word's letters are reordered

parts.note: yet means even, as in 'even more' or 'yet more'

explanation.surface: A further turn of fortune, even after new safeguards are put in.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside YET, giving YNET, which follows S and the rearranged FATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety net is any fallback provision guarding against failure, a precaution.

clue.text: In essence, miller's conclusion it's what he needs

indicators.note: something placed in a word sits inside its letters

parts.note: the gist is the essence of something

indicators.note: a word's conclusion is its final letter

explanation.surface: Essentially, the miller concludes, this is exactly what he requires.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the miller in the wordplay: 'he' is the miller, and 'all grist to the mill' is the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Grist is grain brought to be ground, the raw material a miller works on.

clue.text: Money in many countries held by entrepreneur, ostensibly

indicators.note: letters held by a phrase are contained within it, spanning its words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A businessman apparently holds cash used across many nations.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the shared currency of most European Union member states.

clue.text: Student of biology, for example, arranged insects with it

indicators.note: arranging items puts them in a new order, so these letters are set out differently

parts.note: the letters of insects plus it

explanation.surface: A biology student lays out pinned insects in a collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Biology is one example of a science, so someone studying it is a scientist.

clue.text: Players stupidly sent a singularly useless instrument?

indicators.note: acting stupidly means acting without order, so the following letters are scrambled

parts.note: the cast are the players in a production

explanation.surface: Musicians foolishly despatched an instrument that was no use at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singularly' seems to mean 'remarkably', but it means 'in the singular': one castanet alone cannot be clicked against its partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Castanets work as a pair of shells clapped together, so a single one is a useless instrument.

clue.text: Bit of incidental information is turned over with pleasure

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the short word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A trivial detail is gleefully passed over.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidelight is a piece of information that casts incidental light on a subject.

clue.text: Suitable unit alternating with CID, given explanatory title

indicators.note: alternating places the pieces turn about, each slipped between the letters of the other

parts.note: taken as written, the detective branch of the UK police

explanation.surface: A fitting police squad, taking turns with the detectives, is given a heading.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters C, I and D take turns with the two words: C, APT, I, ONE, D.
explanation.definitionFit: A captioned picture has been given a short explanatory title or heading.

clue.text: Little agreement

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a pact or treaty

explanation.walkthrough: Two words that look like one phrase about a small deal are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means small and neatly packed; as a noun it means a formal pact between parties.

clue.text: Intimate letters from Rome redistributed in city further south

indicators.note: redistributing hands things out afresh, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: a pal is an intimate friend
the letters of the city's name rearranged

explanation.surface: Private correspondence from the capital is forwarded to a more southerly Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intimate' looks like a verb or adjective for the letters; it is a noun, a close friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Palermo, the Sicilian capital, lies well to the south of Rome.

clue.text: Hard-hearted prejudice reflected in how Indian addressed European

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirrored, so the word is read backwards
a heart sits in the middle, so this letter goes into the centre of the other word

parts.note: H abbreviates hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Callous bigotry shows in the way colonial India spoke to Europeans.
explanation.definitionFit: Sahib was the respectful title Indians used for European men in colonial times, roughly meaning sir or master.

clue.text: Endlessly awful time in retreat

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A dreadful, never-ending stretch spent in seclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' looks like a verb; it is the noun, a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideout is a secluded place to retreat to and stay hidden.

clue.text: Important judge hiding old intolerant attitudes

indicators.note: something hidden is tucked inside, so this letter goes between the words

parts.note: to try a case is to judge it

explanation.surface: A senior judge conceals his outdated prejudices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Important judge' looks like a single figure, but the two words go either side of O.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigotry is intolerance of other people's views or identities.

clue.text: Bishop, for instance, protecting one left in site of Italian cathedral

indicators.note: to protect is to surround, so these letters go inside the other word

parts.note: a bishop is one of the men in chess
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A bishop guards a lone survivor at a famous Italian church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop' seems ecclesiastical, fitting the cathedral, but it is a chess piece, one of the men.
explanation.definitionFit: Milan is home to the Duomo, its great Gothic cathedral.

clue.text: E.g. old cop I redeployed as tracker, say

indicators.note: redeployed units are posted in new positions, so the letters take new places

explanation.surface: A veteran officer is reassigned to tracking duties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks the definition as an example: a tracker is one kind of police dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Police dogs are trained to follow scents, so a tracker is one example.

clue.text: Safe one robbed for Paul's benefit?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: criminal slang for a strongbox
second meaning: from the saying about robbing one apostle to pay another

explanation.surface: A strongbox is raided so that someone else gains.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'rob Peter to pay Paul' means taking from one to give to another. In old criminal slang a peter is a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A peterman is a safecracker, from peter as slang for safe; the apostle is the one robbed in the proverb.

clue.text: Preserve a lake as waterway

parts.note: to can food is to preserve it

explanation.surface: Conservationists want a lake kept as a navigable channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal is a man-made channel for boats, an artificial waterway.

clue.text: Way to counter being cut off if trial must be rearranged

definitions.text: Way to counter being cut off

indicators.note: rearranging changes the order, so the letters given are shuffled into another word

parts.note: every letter of these two words

explanation.surface: A court case that gets interrupted will have to be rescheduled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' suggests a broken hearing; it means a place isolated by siege or blockade, as Berlin was in 1948.
explanation.definitionFit: An airlift flies in supplies to a place blockaded or cut off by land.

clue.text: Craft of forceful diplomacy

parts.note: surface reading: the art or skill of a strong-arm negotiator
setter's reading: a vessel, the armed boat that gives its name to diplomacy backed by threat of force

explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' reads as skill, but it is a boat; the phrase recalls a famous kind of intimidating foreign policy.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunboat diplomacy means coercing other states by displaying naval firepower, so the vessel is literally its craft.

clue.text: Part of pig or horse

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pig's foot, eaten as food
second meaning: a horse bred for trotting races

explanation.surface: A farmyard question: is this bit from the pig or from the horse?
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's trotter is its foot, and a trotter is also a harness-racing horse that trots.

clue.text: Author mostly told story with no end of flair

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
having no end of a word means its final letter is taken away from the other

parts.note: the end of this word, taken away from the previous one

explanation.surface: A writer narrated a tale, mostly, but without any real flair.
explanation.walkthrough: TOLD loses its D; STORY loses R, the last letter of flair.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo Tolstoy was the Russian novelist who wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina.
